title: Jason da Silva Castanheira
text:
My research is broadly interested in tackling how brain rhythms can explain our unique behavioural patterns and subjective experiences

Attention & Consciousness
Our senses are constantly bombarded with information. We must select a subset of this information to preferentially process. I am interested in these attention-orienting processes. Specifically, my research examines i) how different types of attention systems interact with one another and ii) how we construe our environment in service of our goals.
Recently, I have examined attention biases in how people construe problems for planning. Using computational modelling, I’ve explored visuospatial attentional biases in how we construe problems both tied to perception and from our imaginations.



Studying how people select task-relevant information to construe


In the future, I wish to explore:

How people construe problems from their imagination.
• How people simultaneously orient their attention internally and externally to guide adaptive behaviours.
How construal processes go awry in mental health.



Brain Rhythms
Since the invention of EEG, over a century ago, people have been interested in measuring brain rhythms. This isn’t always easy! Brain activity is characterized by several brain rhythms and by background noise. This background noise, however, relates to people’s age and predicts cognitive performance. Yet, the question remains: how do we measure rhythmic and arrhythmic brain activity and how do these components contribute to our subjective experiences?



Rhythmic and arrhythmic brain activity, image adapted from Luc Wilson


We have made available tools to parameterize the neural power spectrum using Bayesian model selection and time-resolved estimates of arrhythmic and rhythmic brain activity.
I’ve also explored, using simulations, best practices for detrending neural power spectra. Here, we find that modelled rhythmic power is the best way to decompose arrhythmic and rhythmic components without introducing spurious relationships between the components.



Methodologies for quantifying arrhythmic and rhythmic brain activity




Inter-individual differences
We all have the intuition that we are unique individuals; but how unique is your brain (activity)? Researchers, including myself, have pioneered techniques to study this question.
Finn and colleagues in 2015 first put forward the idea of a brain-fingerprint: brain activity that differentiates you from a cohort of people. Much like a fingerprint left by your hand we can distinguish people from one another using these brain-fingerprints. But unlike the fingerprints left by your hand, brain-fingerprints relate to inter-individual differences in cognitive performance and are shaped by demographic variables.
My work on brain-fingerprinting established that individuals can be differentiated from one another using brief 30-second recordings of brain activity. People’s unique brain rhythms are remarkably stable across months!
I’ve also shown that monozygotic (identical) twins have very similar brain-fingerprints. This suggests that brain-fingerprints are heritable! Unique patterns of brain rhythms also relate to patterns of cortical gene expression.



Rhythmic brain activity distinguishes between people and is related to cortical gene expression


The features that set us apart from one another also differ across the lifespan, with rhythmic brain activity being particularly good at distinguishing individuals across the entire lifespan.



Brain-fingerprinting across the lifespan


Moving forward, I wish to explore:

What life-changing moments permanently change our unique brain rhythms?
How do brain rhythms relate to how we perceive and experience the world?

Below please find a summary of helpful (teaching) resources.

How to measure brain rhythms
Brain activity is composed of both rhythmic and arrhythmic components. Researchers theorize that both components are generated by different neural mechanisms and are believed to behaviour independently. I am interested in i) how to best quantify rhythmic and arrhythmic brain activity and ii) how does arrhythmic and rhythmic brain activity relate to our subjective experiences.



Schematic of time resolved arrhythmic and rhythmic parameterization


For a detail tutorial on how to parameterize the neural power spectrum please visit the Brainstorm tutorial pages for ms-specparam. Please visit the Spectral Parameterization Resolved in Time (SPRiNT) if you would like to learn more about time resolved measures of arrhythmic and rhythmic brain activity.


How to brain-fingerprint?

title: Jason da Silva Castanheira
text:
About me
 I am a postdoctoral research fellow at UCL studying consciousness, attention, and inter-individual differences with Prof. Stephen Fleming. My work blends cognitive science, computational modelling, and neurophysiology to understand how brain rhythms support our unique subjective experiences.
I completed my PhD with Prof. Sylvain Baillet at McGill University in the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI). There I studied how individuals brain activity is characteristic to them, much like a fingerprint left by your hand. My thesis, MEG, myself, and I: Understanding inter-individual diversity of neurophysiological brain activity was awarded the Governor General’s Gold Medal for outstanding doctoral thesis in the Natural Sciences.
